summary: This best current practice gives guidelines for authors and reviewers of specifications containing YANG modules. The recommendations and procedures aim to improve interoperability and usability of NETCONF and RESTCONF implementations. It was later replaced by RFC 9907.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language used to describe the data a network device can be configured with. The language allows a lot of freedom, and this document is the set of house rules the IETF agreed on so that models written by different people look alike and can be implemented the same way. It covers how to name things, which defaults to leave out, how to describe types, and how to write the surrounding document.

subtitle: The rules of house for writing and reviewing a YANG data model so that other people can use it.

tldr.problem: YANG lets an author leave many things optional, and lets an author use constructs that a server is allowed to ignore. Two modules that both obey the YANG specification can still be hard to read, hard to review and hard to implement together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out usage guidelines for module names, prefixes, identifiers, defaults, conditional statements, namespaces, top-level data and data types, together with rules for how the document around the module should be written.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice document that obsoletes RFC 6087. It was later updated by RFC 8819, which adds YANG module tags, and has since been obsoleted by RFC 9907.

today: RFC 8407 was published in October 2018 as a Best Current Practice document and obsoletes RFC 6087. It was updated by RFC 8819, which adds YANG module tags, and has since been obsoleted by RFC 9907, which carries on the same guidelines.

sections.title: Why These Guidelines Exist
sections.content:
The standardization of network configuration interfaces for use with network configuration management protocols, such as the Network Configuration Protocol and the RESTCONF protocol, requires a modular set of data models that can be reused and extended over time. YANG is used to define the data structures, protocol operations and notification content used within a NETCONF or RESTCONF server, and a server that supports a particular YANG module supports the client operations indicated by the specific content defined in that module.

Many YANG constructs are defined as optional to use, such as the description statement. In order to make YANG modules more useful, it is desirable to define a set of usage guidelines that entails a higher level of compliance than the minimum level defined in the YANG specification. YANG also allows constructs such as infinite length identifiers and string values, or top-level mandatory nodes, that a compliant server is not required to support, and only constructs that all servers are required to support can be used in IETF YANG modules.

The guidelines are intended to be used by authors and reviewers to improve the readability and interoperability of published YANG data models. The RFC is explicit that it is not a YANG tutorial, and that the reader is expected to know the data modeling language before implementing the guidance.

The document also defines its own terms. A published module is a stable release, such as a Request for Comments, while an unpublished module is an unstable release, such as an Internet-Draft that is a work in progress subject to change at any time. A YANG fragment is a set of statements not intended to represent a complete module, used to give an example, and the invalid syntax of three dots is sometimes used to show where more statements would be present in a real module. A YANG tree diagram is a diagram representing the contents of a module, as defined in the tree diagram specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The language itself lets you leave things out and lets you use features a device may ignore. This document is the stricter house style the IETF agreed on, so that a reader of one model can guess how another is written, and so that two independent implementations end up doing the same thing.

sections.title: How the Document Should Be Written
sections.content:
The RFC's general documentation guidelines cover the material around the module rather than the module itself, and they begin with the rule that all guidelines for Internet-Draft authors must be followed.

The section covers the module copyright and the code components, the terminology section, tree diagrams and the narrative sections of a document, the definitions section, the security considerations section, the IANA considerations section and the references sections. It also covers validation tools, module extraction tools and module usage examples.

Two points are worth drawing out. The security considerations section of a document containing YANG is required to be present, and it must cover the ways in which the data model could be used maliciously. And the IANA considerations section must contain the template needed to register the module, because the module name, its namespace and its prefix all have to be registered before the module can be published.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the rules are about the document rather than the code: the terms it uses, the diagrams that show the shape of the data, the security discussion, and the details IANA needs in order to register the module's name and namespace.

sections.title: Module Names, Prefixes and Identifiers
sections.content:
Normative modules contained in Standards Track documents must be named according to the guidelines in the IANA considerations section of the YANG specification. A distinctive word or abbreviation, such as a protocol name or a working group abbreviation, should be used in the module name, and if new definitions extend one or more existing modules, the same word or abbreviation should be reused instead of creating a new one. All published module names must be unique; for a module published in an RFC this is guaranteed by IANA, but for unpublished modules the authors need to check that no other work in progress uses the same name. Example modules are non-normative and should be named with the prefix example-.

The RFC suggests that a stable prefix be selected that represents the entire organization. All normative YANG modules published by the IETF must begin with the prefix ietf-, and another standards organization, such as the IEEE, might use the prefix ieee- for all its modules. Once a module name is published it must not be reused, even if the RFC containing it is reclassified as Historic. A module name cannot be changed in YANG, and doing so would be treated as a new module rather than a name change.

On prefixes, YANG definitions are scoped by the module that contains them, so definitions from several modules can be used even when their names are not unique. Prefixes are never used for built-in data types and YANG keywords, a prefix must be used for any external statement, and the proper module prefix must be used for identifiers imported from other modules and for identifiers included from a submodule. The local module prefix should be used rather than no prefix in all path expressions, and must be used in all default statements for an identityref or instance-identifier data type. Prefix values should be short but are also likely to be unique.

Identifiers in published modules must be between 1 and 64 characters long. They should follow a consistent naming pattern throughout the module, and only lowercase letters, numbers and dashes should be used, with uppercase characters, the period and the underscore permitted when the identifier represents a well-known value that uses them. Child nodes within a container or list should not replicate the parent identifier. Identifiers should not carry special semantics that identify data modelling properties, because only YANG statements and YANG extension statements convey machine-readable properties: naming an object config or state does not change whether it is configuration data or state data.
sections.plainLanguage: Names have to be unique and stable. Once a module is published its name is taken for good, and changing it would count as a different module. Inside the module, names use lower case with dashes, stay under sixty-four characters, and must not pretend to mean something the language does not actually assign.

sections.title: Defaults, Conditions and Namespaces
sections.content:
In general, substatements containing very common default values should not be present, because writing them everywhere makes the module hard to read. The RFC lists the seven statements whose defaults are common enough to leave out: config with a default of true, mandatory with a default of false, max-elements with a default of unbounded, min-elements with a default of 0, ordered-by with a default of system, status with a default of current, and yin-element with a default of false.

On conditional statements, a module may be partitioned in several ways using the if-feature and when statements. If a data definition is optional depending on server support for a NETCONF or RESTCONF protocol capability, then a feature statement should be defined, and the if-feature statement should then be used to reference the optional data definition. If any notification data, or any data definition for a non-configuration data node, is not mandatory, the server may or may not be required to return an instance of it, so any conditional requirements for returning the data node in a notification payload or retrieval request must be documented somewhere, for example with a when or if-feature statement, or explained in a description statement. If any if-feature statements apply to a list node, the same if-feature statements must apply to any key leaf nodes for the list, and there must not be any if-feature statements applied to key leafs that do not also apply to the parent list node. There should not be any when statements applied to a key leaf node, because a when statement for an ancestor of the key leaf can have exactly the same effect and is redundant.

On namespaces, it is recommended that only valid YANG modules be included in documents, whether or not the modules are published yet, so that the module compiles correctly, early implementors can use it without picking a random value for the XML namespace, and independent implementations can interoperate because they use the same namespace value. Until a URI is assigned by IANA, a proposed namespace URI must be provided for the namespace statement, chosen so that it is not likely to collide with other YANG namespaces, and module names, prefixes and URI strings already in the YANG Module Names registry must not be used. The standard form is a URN prefix string followed by a colon and the module name, and the prefix string to use for published and unpublished YANG modules is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:.
sections.plainLanguage: Leave out the defaults, because everybody knows them. Say clearly when a piece of data only exists if the device supports it, and say so in a standard way so a client can ask. And give the module a namespace that will not clash with anyone else's, using the standard form so it can be recognised.

sections.title: Top-Level Data and Data Types
sections.content:
The top-level data organization should be considered carefully, in advance, because the model designer has to consider how the functionality for a given protocol or protocol family will grow over time. The separation of configuration data and operational state should be considered carefully, and it is sometimes useful to define separate top-level containers for configuration and non-configuration data. For some existing top-level data nodes, configuration data was not in scope, so only one container representing operational state was created.

The number of top-level data nodes within a module should be minimized, because it is often useful to retrieve related information within a single subtree, and if data is too distributed it becomes difficult to retrieve all at once. The names and data organization should reflect persistent information such as the name of a protocol, and should not use the name of the working group, because that may change over time. A mandatory database data definition is a node that a client must provide for the database to be valid, while the server is not required to provide a value. Top-level database data definitions must not be mandatory, because a mandatory node at the top level immediately makes the database invalid, which can happen when the server boots or when a module is loaded dynamically at runtime.

On data types, the choice of a built-in type, an existing derived type or a new derived type is very subjective, so few requirements are given, but the most appropriate built-in type for the application should be used, and the signed numeric types int8, int16, int32 and int64 should not be used unless negative values are allowed for the desired semantics.

The RFC then works through the choices. If the set of values is fixed and controlled by a single naming authority, an enumeration type should be used; if extensibility of enumerated values is required, the identityref type should be used instead of an enumeration or other built-in type. For string types, if a machine-readable pattern can be defined for the desired semantics, one or more pattern statements should be present, a single-quoted string should be used to specify the pattern because a double-quoted string can modify the content, and any known limitations of the pattern such as false negative or false positive matches should be documented. If the length of the string is required to be bounded in all implementations, a length statement must be present. For numeric types, if the values allowed by the intended semantics differ from those allowed by the unbounded intrinsic type, a range statement should be present. For enumeration and bits types, the semantics for each enum or bit should be documented with a separate description statement.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the shape of the data shallow, so that a client can fetch everything it needs in one go, and never require a client to fill in a top-level value, because that would make the running configuration invalid. When choosing a type, use the narrowest one that fits: a fixed list of values, a value that others may extend, a pattern for text, a range for numbers, and a description for each value.

sections.title: Registration and the Security Note
sections.content:
The registration in the ns subregistry of the IETF XML Registry was detailed in RFC 6087 and has been updated by IANA to reference this document. It requests the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-template, with the IESG as the registrant contact and the XML field marked as not applicable, the requested URI being an XML namespace.

The corresponding assignment in the YANG Module Names registry has also been updated by IANA, and this document has been added as a reference for that registry itself, because it contains the template needed for registration. The name is ietf-template, the namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-template, the prefix is temp and the reference is RFC 8407.

The Security Considerations section is short. The document defines documentation guidelines for NETCONF or RESTCONF content defined with the YANG data modeling language, and therefore does not introduce any new or increased security risks into the management system. The security consequences of a particular data model have to be covered in the document that carries that model.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a list of every YANG module name and the namespace it uses, and this document holds the template that goes with each new entry. On security, the point is that the guidelines themselves do not create risk; the risk belongs to the model, and has to be written up in the document that defines the model.
